body_md: Profile with `cargo flamegraph`: samples stacks into SVG. Run on release binary. Wide bars are hot paths. Fix allocation and cloning first — they dominate.
code:
$ cargo install flamegraph
$ cargo flamegraph --bin app
# open flamegraph.svg
hook: Find the 5% of code eating 95% of time — flamegraph shows it.
output:
// cargo flamegraph --bin app
// → flamegraph.svg: widest bars are the hot paths (profile release)

quiz.explain: A profiler samples call stacks; each box's width is the share of samples it appears in, so wide boxes are hot code.
options: Log lines grouped by module and level
Test durations plotted against build time
Sampled stacks; width is share of time
Memory addresses of every allocation

trap: Profiling debug builds misleads; always release + debuginfo.

body_md: `perf stat` counts cycles, cache-misses, branch-misses. `perf record/report` pinpoints symbols. High miss rates mean layout or branch fixes, not micro-tweaks.
code:
$ perf stat ./target/release/app
$ perf record ./target/release/app
$ perf report
hook: Cache misses cost 100x — perf counts what profilers hide.
output:
// perf stat: cycles, cache-misses, branch-misses per run
// → perf record/report pinpoints the hot symbols

quiz.explain: perf stat reads CPU hardware counters for cycles, cache misses, and branch misses. Timers show slowness but not why.
options: Time each function with Instant::now
perf stat reading hardware counters
cargo test --release with timings on
Count allocations with a custom allocator
quiz.q: How do you measure cache misses?

trap: Tuning without counters optimizes wrong function.

body_md: Swap allocators for throughput: `#[global_allocator] static A: tikv_jemallocator::Jemalloc;` or mimalloc. Gains 10-30% on alloc-heavy servers. Measure with benches.
hook: One line, 20% faster server — swap the allocator.
output: // compiles with mimalloc: global allocator swapped (measure first)

quiz.explain: A static annotated #[global_allocator] replaces the system allocator for every Box, Vec, and String in the program.
options: Declare it with #[global_allocator]
Set RUST_ALLOCATOR=mimalloc at runtime
Add mimalloc to [profile.release]
Call mimalloc::init() at the top of main
quiz.q: How do you switch a binary to mimalloc?

takeaway: Allocator choice matters for alloc-heavy apps.
trap: Jemalloc static bloat on tiny binaries; measure binary size.

body_md: SIMD processes 4-8 lanes at once. `std::simd` (nightly) or `wide` crate auto-vectorizes loops. Check with `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native"` for AVX gains.
hook: Do 8 adds in one instruction — SIMD is free speed.

quiz.explain: SIMD instructions apply one operation to 4-8+ packed values at once, so a vectorized loop handles several elements per instruction.
options: Runs each loop iteration on its own thread
Speculatively runs both sides of a branch
Splits one value across several registers
Applies one instruction to several lanes

trap: Unaligned loads or branches kill vectorization silently.

body_md: `#![no_std]` drops std for embedded: use `core` + `alloc`. No threads, no files. Add panic handler, `cortex-m-rt` target. Allocations via `heapless` fixed buffers.
hook: Rust on a $2 chip with no OS — no_std makes it possible.
output: // compiles for embedded target: core only, own panic handler + #[entry]

quiz.explain: std needs an OS for threads and files; no_std builds on core, which runs anywhere, and alloc adds heap types if you supply an allocator.
options: Use std with the panic=abort profile
#![no_std], building on core (and alloc)
Compile to WASM and run in an interpreter
Statically link std against musl libc
quiz.q: How do you run Rust bare-metal with no OS?

trap: Using std types (File, Thread) in no_std fails to compile.

body_md: Cut allocations: reuse buffers with `clear()`, `String::with_capacity`, `BytesMut` pools. Clone in loop is top perf killer — borrow or `Cow` instead.
hook: Buffer reuse: the fastest allocation is the one you skip.

quiz.explain: clear() drops contents but keeps capacity, so the next iteration reuses memory. Cloning and boxing add allocations instead.
options: Clone inputs so each iteration owns its data
Box each value so moves only copy a pointer
Reuse a buffer: clear() keeps its capacity
Shrink Vecs with shrink_to_fit each pass
quiz.q: How do you cut allocator pressure in a hot loop?

trap: String::new in loop reallocs every iteration.

body_md: Release tuning: `lto = true`, `codegen-units = 1`, `panic = "abort"`, `strip = true` in Cargo.toml. PGO via `RUSTFLAGS="-Cprofile-generate"` adds 10-20%.
hook: Release profile: three Cargo.toml lines that speed your binary.
output:
# release: LTO + one codegen unit + stripped
# → smaller, faster binary; ~3x slower builds

quiz.explain: LTO optimizes across crates and one codegen unit lets LLVM inline everywhere, at the cost of slower builds. opt-level z targets size.
options: lto = true and codegen-units = 1
debug = true for full symbol info
opt-level = "z" with incremental on
codegen-units = 256 to parallelize
quiz.q: Which release settings maximize runtime speed?

takeaway: Tune release profile for size and speed.
trap: LTO slows builds 3x; gate behind release pipeline.

body_md: Zero-copy parsing with `&str` slices, `bytes::Bytes` refcounted views, `serde` borrowed `&'a str`. Avoid `to_string` in parsers — slice the input instead.
hook: Parse gigabytes without copying a byte — zero-copy.
output: // compiles: returns a zero-copy &str slice of the input

quiz.explain: Borrowed &str slices point into the original buffer, so no bytes are copied. to_string, String, and format! each allocate.
options: Call to_string() on each token you keep
Return &str slices borrowed from the input
Collect tokens into a Vec<String> first
Build each field with format! exactly once
quiz.q: How do you parse input without allocating?

takeaway: Slice inputs; avoid owned copies in parsers.
trap: Returning borrowed slice tied to temp input dangles.

body_md: Async perf: pool connections (`deadpool`), batch with `buffered`, compress with `tower` layers. Monitor with `tokio-metrics`. Backpressure beats unbounded spawn.
code:
// let pool = deadpool_postgres::Pool::new(mgr, 16);
// let obj = pool.get().await.unwrap();
hook: 100k requests, 16 DB slots — pooling plus backpressure wins.
output: // with deadpool: get().await lends 1 of 16 conns; waits when exhausted

quiz.explain: A pool reuses connections and caps how many run at once, so excess requests wait instead of piling up and exhausting the DB.
options: Open a fresh connection per request
Spawn one unbounded task per request
Pool connections and bound concurrency
Add sleep() between queries to pace them
quiz.q: How do you scale async DB access under load?

takeaway: Pool, batch, and bound async workloads.
trap: Unbounded spawn per request OOMs under burst.

body_md: Size matters: `cargo bloat --release` finds fat deps. Prefer `no_std` crates, `default-features = false`, `opt-level = "z"`. One heavy dep can double binary.
hook: Binary bloat: find which crates fatten your release build.
output:
// cargo bloat --release -n 20
// → table of heaviest crates; trim default-features first

quiz.explain: cargo bloat ranks crates and functions by bytes in the final binary. --timings shows compile time, not output size.
options: Run cargo bloat on a release build
Run cargo build --timings on the crate
Run cargo test with size reporting on
Run cargo clippy with pedantic lints
quiz.q: How do you find what bloats binary size?

takeaway: Audit binary size; trim default features.
trap: Disabling features blindly breaks API; check docs.
